methodNote: Genealogy links are editorial research paths, not claims of one-to-one legal derivation. Early debates are connected to later constitutional families only where the processed record shows the same constitutional problem or design question.

families.label: Preamble
families.title: Constitutional ideals and popular authority
families.summary: Popular sovereignty, justice, liberty, equality and the political character of the future Republic appear first as constitutional objectives before becoming part of the Constitution's opening statement.

roots.title: Objectives Resolution moved
roots.note: Jawaharlal Nehru places sovereignty, justice, equality, freedoms and safeguards into one constitutional programme.

roots.title: Objectives Resolution adopted
roots.note: The Assembly accepts the Resolution as its constitutional direction after the December–January debate sequence.

roots.title: High-level ideals begin becoming enforceable clauses
roots.note: The April rights debate shows how broad constitutional promises have to be separated into legal rights, restrictions and non-justiciable principles.

families.label: Article 1 family
families.title: India, the Union and its constituent territories
families.summary: The early Assembly repeatedly tests what political community is being constituted, how Indian States enter it and what belongs to the Union before the final territorial provision exists.

roots.title: The future Union is described at the level of constitutional objectives
roots.note: The Resolution identifies the territorial and political community before the detailed federal structure is settled.

roots.title: States Negotiating Committee created
roots.note: The Assembly creates a route for negotiating how Indian States will participate in constitution-making.

roots.title: Representatives of Indian States begin taking seats
roots.note: The political community becomes institutionally broader while the Union-subject framework remains deliberately provisional.

roots.title: Union Constitution Committee authorised
roots.note: The Assembly creates a dedicated body to report on the main principles of the Union Constitution.

families.label: Article 14 family
families.title: Equality before law and equal protection
families.summary: Equality moves from an objective into a drafting problem: whether formal equality is enough, what discrimination means and how social hierarchy affects constitutional protection.

roots.title: Equality appears in the Objectives Resolution
roots.note: Equality is initially stated as a constitutional aim rather than a finished legal rule.

roots.title: Members test equality against social and political exclusion
roots.note: Claims from minorities, Scheduled Castes, Adivasis and other groups make the social content of equality unavoidable.

roots.title: Equality enters the interim Fundamental Rights discussion
roots.note: The House begins converting equality into legal language and debating its relationship with discrimination and social structure.

families.label: Article 16 family
families.title: Equal opportunity in public employment
families.summary: The 30 April debate makes the equality problem concrete: open public employment must coexist with the need to correct severe under-representation.

roots.title: Public-employment equality and corrective reservation are debated together
roots.note: The Assembly tests how a general equality rule can coexist with measures for communities inadequately represented in public services.

families.label: Article 17 family
families.title: Abolition of untouchability
families.summary: The rights debate makes clear that legal equality cannot ignore entrenched caste exclusion. Members explicitly connect untouchability to the social structure the Constitution must confront.

roots.title: Scheduled Caste claims expose the limits of abstract equality
roots.note: The debate on safeguards and representation shows why a Constitution must address historically structured exclusion rather than rely on general language alone.

roots.title: P. R. Thakur links untouchability directly to caste
roots.note: The rights debate treats untouchability as a constitutional problem embedded in social hierarchy.

families.label: Article 19 family
families.title: Freedoms and their permissible restrictions
families.summary: The Assembly does not debate liberty in the abstract for long. Speech, movement, association, residence and occupation quickly become arguments about public order, emergency, morality and legitimate regulation.

roots.title: Freedoms appear in the Objectives Resolution
roots.note: Civil liberties enter the constitutional programme before their legal limitations are defined.

roots.title: Members question whether restrictions can consume the right
roots.note: Somnath Lahiri and others challenge rights language that appears broad in promise but narrow in operation.

roots.title: Freedom clauses are tested against public order and regulation
roots.note: The House works through how constitutional freedoms coexist with State power in emergencies and in the public interest.

families.label: Articles 23–24 family
families.title: Forced labour and child labour protections
families.summary: The 1 May sitting shows why anti-exploitation rights require careful drafting: a ban on forced labour must not accidentally prohibit legitimate compulsory public service, while child labour raises a distinct protective question.

roots.title: Forced-labour clause is remitted for reconsideration
roots.note: The Assembly identifies a drafting conflict between prohibiting forced labour and preserving the possibility of compulsory service for public purposes.

roots.title: Child labour enters the same anti-exploitation field
roots.note: The debate distinguishes protection of children from the separate problem of forced adult labour and compulsory service.

families.label: Articles 25–28 family
families.title: Freedom of conscience and religion
families.summary: Religious liberty is immediately tested against coercion, propagation, family authority, minors, social reform and the regulatory role of the State.

roots.title: Conscience and propagation are debated with limits
roots.note: Members ask how religious freedom should interact with coercion, public regulation and reform.

roots.title: Conversion of minors exposes a hard boundary question
roots.note: The House confronts the relationship among personal conscience, parental authority and protection against coercion.

families.label: Articles 29–30 family
families.title: Cultural and educational rights
families.summary: Minority protection evolves from general safeguards into concrete questions about language, culture, educational institutions and the balance between common citizenship and community autonomy.

roots.title: Minority security is tied to the legitimacy of the constitutional settlement
roots.note: Members debate whether unity requires reassurance, safeguards and political accommodation.

roots.title: Advisory Committee receives minority-safeguard work
roots.note: Minority questions are moved into a specialised committee structure rather than left as general promises.

roots.title: Language, culture and educational institutions reach the House
roots.note: The debate tests how common citizenship can coexist with minority cultural and educational autonomy.

families.label: Article 32 family
families.title: Constitutional remedies
families.summary: The April rights debate repeatedly returns to the practical question behind every guarantee: what can an ordinary citizen actually do when the State violates it?

roots.title: Rights are separated from non-justiciable principles
roots.note: The distinction forces the House to decide which constitutional promises must be judicially enforceable.

roots.title: Members ask whether poor citizens can actually use constitutional remedies
roots.note: Ranga and Sidhwa expose the distance between a formal legal remedy and an accessible one.

families.label: Part IV family
families.title: Non-justiciable social and economic principles
families.summary: One of the most consequential early design choices is the separation between judicially enforceable rights and social-economic goals that guide the State without creating the same immediate court remedy.

roots.title: The House confronts the justiciable / non-justiciable divide
roots.note: Members dispute whether major social and economic claims should sit outside the enforceable-rights category.

roots.title: P. R. Thakur challenges the weakness of unenforceable economic guarantees
roots.note: The debate makes explicit that constitutional importance and judicial enforceability are different design choices.
